knowledge_type_note: Terminology, not a motif. It names a STATE of the board, not a move or a method. The tactics that exploit it (fork, discovered attack) are the motifs; this is the condition that makes them pay.

history.notes: 'En prise' is a French borrowing in English chess writing since at least the nineteenth century; no origin research has been done and no single coiner is claimed. 'Hanging' has no established first use in the sources consulted.

engine_era_note: Entirely mechanical and unaffected by engine-era revision. Static exchange evaluation is the standard test and is what this codebase uses.

preconditions: The exchange sequence on its square wins material for the attacker
indicators_for: The piece has no defender at all
It is attacked more times than it is defended
Its only defender is pinned, overloaded, or would be deflected by the capture
indicators_against: Recapture regains equal or greater material — an even trade is not a hanging piece
Taking it walks into a stronger counter-tactic
It is bait: the capture opens a line or removes a defender the opponent wants gone
The piece was ALREADY winnable before this move, so the move is not what hung it
false_positive_traps: A defended piece attacked once is not hanging; count both sides of the exchange.
A nominal defender that is pinned does not defend. SEE catches this; a naive defender count does not.
Material already loose before the move is not this move's doing — reporting it makes the move look worse than it was.

typical_plans: Take it, after checking the recapture sequence and any counter-tactic
tactical_consequences: Supplies the second target that makes a fork or discovered attack pay

exceptions: A hanging piece may be a sacrifice offered on purpose. SEE says the material is winnable; it does not say taking is right.
In a lost position, giving material to reach a fortress or a perpetual can be correct.
limitations: Purely material. It says nothing about whether taking is best.
misconceptions: That a piece with a defender cannot be hanging. It can — if the defender is pinned or overloaded, or if it is attacked twice and defended once.
That every hanging piece should be taken.

examples.note: A clean instance: the detector reports hangingPiece and nothing else, for the move Nf6. Two things are verified here and a third is not. VERIFIED: findMotifs() in blind-chess.html reports the motif — and that detector, not this system, is the authority on whether a motif is present. ALSO VERIFIED: Nf6 is the recorded solution of a shipped puzzle, and tools/generate_puzzles.js only admits a position when one move is objectively best by a wide margin at confirmation depth, so the move carries engine backing by construction rather than by a separate search here. NOT claimed: that the motif is the whole reason the move wins. Provenance: the puzzle corpus is engine self-play — a real position from a real game between engines, not a master game.

engine.verdict_note: Inherited validation: this position ships as a puzzle, and the generator's standard is that exactly one move is best by at least GAP_MIN at confirmation depth, re-checked deeper by tools/verify_puzzles.js. The move is therefore engine-verified as best without this base running its own search. The motif label comes from findMotifs, not from the engine — the two are independent and both had to agree for this to be recorded.

by_level.beginner: That piece can just be taken for free — nothing is defending it.
by_level.intermediate: The {piece} on {square} hangs: it is attacked {n} times and defended {m}, so the exchange wins material.
by_level.advanced: Hanging by static exchange evaluation. Check whether the capture is a genuine win or an offer — SEE measures material, not correctness.
by_level.master: En prise. Confirm the defender is real (not pinned or overloaded) and that the capture does not concede a line or a tempo worth more than the material.

by_depth.short: The {piece} on {square} can be taken for free.
by_depth.normal: The {piece} on {square} is hanging — attacked and not adequately defended, so the exchange there wins material.
by_depth.deep: Hanging, or en prise in the older French term. The test is the exchange sequence on the square, not a count of attackers: a defender that is pinned or overloaded does not defend. Distinguish from loose, which means undefended but not yet attacked — that is a future problem rather than a present loss.

explanations.lesson: Before every move, check both sides for pieces that can simply be taken. Below master level this decides more games than every strategic idea combined.

definition_short: A piece that is attacked and can be captured for free — undefended, or defended fewer times than it is attacked.
definition_long:
A piece stands where the opponent can take it and come out ahead. In everyday English it 'hangs'; the traditional French term is EN PRISE, literally 'in a position to be taken'.

Three words are used in this area and the distinction between them is worth keeping:

  EN PRISE — attacked and capturable. Strictly this says nothing about defence, though in living usage it means capturing wins material.
  HANGING — the English equivalent, and in practice the stronger claim: attacked AND undefended, or defended too few times.
  LOOSE — undefended but not necessarily attacked YET. Not a loss today; the raw material of tomorrow's tactic. Recorded separately as `loose-piece`.

The hanging/loose line is the one that carries weight, because it separates a mistake that has already happened from a condition that invites one.

IN THIS CODEBASE: `findMotifs()` emits `hangingPiece` using static exchange evaluation — it reports a piece only where `see(after, square, attacker) > 0`, i.e. the exchange on that square actually wins material, and it explicitly skips anything that was already winnable before the move. That is the strict, correct reading, and it is by far the most common theme in the shipped puzzle set (598 of 788 puzzles).
